'''Edwin Evariste Moïse''' ({{IPAc-en|m|oʊ|ˈ|iː|z}};<ref name="NYT obit" /> December 22, 1918 – December 18, 1998)<ref name="NYT obit">{{cite news |first=Wolfgang |last=Saxon |title=Edwin Evariste Moise, 79, Mathematics Scholar |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D07E2DF143FF93BA15751C1A96E958260 |work=New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |date=2008-12-28 |access-date=2008-09-07}}
</ref><ref name="RootsWeb SSDI">
{{cite web |url=http://ssdi.rootsweb.ancestry.com/cgi-bin/ssdi.cgi |title=Social Security Death Index Interactive Search |access-date=2008-09-14 |publisher=RootsWeb (based on Social Security Administration records)|quote= search for Moise, Edwin E}}
</ref>
was an American mathematician and mathematics education reformer. After his retirement from mathematics he became a [[literary critic]] of 19th-century [[English poetry]] and had several notes published in that field.<ref name="NYT obit" /><ref name="Anderson Fitzpatrick interview">{{cite web |url=http://at.yorku.ca/t/o/p/c/94.htm |title=An Interview of Edwin Moise |access-date=2008-09-08 |last=Anderson |first=Richard D. |author2=Ben Fitzpatrick, Jr |date=1998-06-29 |work=Topology Atlas |publisher=York University |archive-date=2010-03-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100312094833/http://at.yorku.ca/t/o/p/c/94.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Edwin E. Moïse was born December 22, 1918, in [[New Orleans]], [[Louisiana]].<ref name="RootsWeb SSDI" /><ref name="Notices obit">{{cite journal |date=May 1999 |title=Mathematics People |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=46 |issue=5 |pages=573–575 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199905/people.pdf |access-date=2008-09-06 |quote=incorrectly gives December 25 as death date |issn=0002-9920}}</ref>  He graduated from [[Tulane University]] in 1940.<ref name="NYT obit" /> He worked as a [[cryptanalyst]] and Japanese translator for the [[Office of the Chief of Naval Operations]] during [[World War II]].<ref name="NYT obit" /><ref name="ICMI profile">{{cite web |url=http://www.icmihistory.unito.it/portrait/moise.php |title=History of the International Commission on Mathematical Instruction - Profile of Edwin Evariste Moise |access-date=2008-09-08 |last=Kilpatrick |first=Jeremy |date=2007-11-27 |publisher=University of Turin}}</ref>

He received his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in mathematics from the [[University of Texas]] in 1947.<ref name="NYT obit" /> His dissertation was titled "An indecomposable continuum which is homeomorphic to each of its nondegenerate subcontinua," a topic in [[continuum theory]], and was written under the direction of [[Robert Lee Moore]]. In his dissertation Moise coined the term [[pseudo-arc]].<ref name="ICMI profile" /><ref name="Students of Moore">{{cite web |url=http://www.discovery.utexas.edu/rlm/reference/fitzpatrick.html |title=The Students of R.L. Moore |access-date=2008-09-08 |last=Fitzpatrick, Jr. |first=Ben |date=July 2005 |work=Legacy of R. L. Moore |publisher=University of Texas}}</ref>

==Career==
Moïse taught at the [[University of Michigan]] from 1947 to 1960. He was James B. Conant Professor of education and mathematics at [[Harvard University]]  from 1960 to 1971. He held a Distinguished Professorship at [[Queens College, City University of New York]] from 1971 to 1987.<ref name="NYT obit" /><ref name="ICMI profile" />

Moïse started working on the topology of [[3-manifold]]s while at the [[University of Michigan]]. During 1949–1951 he held an appointment at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] during which he proved [[Moise's theorem]] that every 3-manifold can be [[triangulation (topology)|triangulated]] in an essentially unique way.<ref name="ICMI profile" />

Moïse joined the [[School Mathematics Study Group]] when it started in 1958, as a member of the geometry writing team. The team produced several course outlines and sample pages for a 10th grade [[geometry]] course, and then Moïse and Floyd L. Downs wrote a geometry textbook, based on the team's approach, that was published in 1964. The textbook used metric postulates instead of [[Euclidean geometry#Axioms|Euclid's postulates]], a controversial approach supported by some mathematicians such as [[Saunders Mac Lane]] but opposed by others such as Alexander Wittenberg and [[Morris Kline]].<ref name="ICMI profile" />

Moïse was a president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]], a vice-president of the [[American Mathematical Society]], a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and was on the executive committee of the [[International Commission on Mathematical Instruction]].<ref name="NYT obit" /><ref name="ICMI profile" />

Moïse  retired from Queens College in 1987 and started a second career studying 19th century [[English poetry]].<ref name="NYT obit" /> He had six short notes of [[literary criticism]] published.<ref name="Anderson Fitzpatrick interview" />

Moise died in [[New York City]] on December 18, 1998, aged 79.<ref name="NYT obit" /><ref name="RootsWeb SSDI" />
